calls: widened from one metro to the Stroke Belt states. the cleaned Chicago sample was a tiny slice of US tracts, and the hypertension burden is documented across the region.
medication coverage among adults already diagnosed as the treatment outcome, not recorded prevalence. low recorded prevalence can mean less testing rather than less disease.
interquartile rule for flagging high-burden tracts, not z-scores. tract percentages are bounded and right-skewed.
collinear behavioural measures left out of the second model. inactivity, smoking and short sleep are multicollinear with obesity, the predictor of interest.
broke: tract IDs kept losing their leading zero when read as numbers, which silently breaks joins for every state whose FIPS code starts with one.
the first model cell was committed in an erroring state after the medication column was renamed.
the source column name for the treatment measure implied a share of the whole tract population rather than of diagnosed adults. renamed before analysis.
tried: first version was Chicago tracts with HOLC redlining grades. too few tracts survived cleaning, so the team moved to Stroke Belt states and dropped the redlining layer.
not_shown: four-person INFO 2950 group project; the decisions above are the team's
found: Stroke Belt patients travel farther for a hospital stay: a median 10.7 miles from home against 7.3 in the median state outside the Belt, and 14% of stays are more than 30 miles away against 8%. Mississippi is the extreme at 27%. For a time-critical condition like stroke, that distance is part of the disparity.

Rural hospital closures track that distance. Across states, a higher closure rate since 2010 goes with a larger share of stays over 30 miles (Spearman ρ 0.41, p = 0.003). The Belt accounts for 48 of the country's 154 closures.

The Belt splits on Medicaid expansion. Arkansas and Louisiana, the region's early expanders (2014, 2016), had 2 closures between them; the six states that held out through the decade had 46, Tennessee alone 14. This is an association across a handful of states, not a causal estimate, but it matches the reimbursement story: expansion shrinks the uncompensated care that small rural hospitals absorb.
